_meta.description: Prescription-access tiers for amphetamine-class ADHD stimulants (amphetamine, dexamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine/Vyvanse) vs. methylphenidate-class vs. non-stimulant-only. NOT legal or medical advice. Confidence/evidence fields indicate how well-sourced each entry is — treat 'low' confidence entries as needing further verification before relying on them.

tiers.1: At least one amphetamine-class ADHD stimulant (dexamphetamine and/or lisdexamfetamine) is approved and routinely prescribable under controlled-substance regulations. Brand availability (e.g. Adderall specifically) does not matter for this tier.
tiers.2: Amphetamine-class ADHD stimulants are not approved or generally unavailable; methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta) is available, possibly with heavy restrictions on quantity/duration.
tiers.3: Amphetamine-class unavailable AND methylphenidate-class also unavailable/unapproved; only non-stimulant options (atomoxetine, clonidine, guanfacine, etc.)
tiers.4: Effectively no approved ADHD pharmacological treatment infrastructure / unclear or unregulated
tiers.unknown: Not yet researched, or researched but evidence only covers travel/import rules rather than domestic prescribing — insufficient to assign a tier

field_definitions.confidence: high | medium | low — how well the evidence supports this specific tier assignment
field_definitions.evidence: government (regulator/formulary/law) | peer_review (published study) | clinical (named practitioner/clinic) | community (advocacy org, forum, travel blog) | mixed
field_definitions.approved: booleans for whether each drug class is approved/routinely prescribable domestically; null = not established
field_definitions.last_verified: year-month this entry's sources were checked

US.notes: Schedule II controlled substance; Adderall, dexamphetamine, and Vyvanse all routinely prescribable.

CA.notes: General knowledge, not independently re-verified against Health Canada this session; regulatory pattern closely mirrors the US.

GB.notes: Elvanse (lisdexamfetamine) and dexamfetamine both licensed and prescribable. Adderall brand specifically is not marketed there, which does not affect this tier.

AU.notes: Schedule 8 controlled drug; dexamphetamine and lisdexamfetamine both prescribable under strict specialist-authority rules. Not independently re-verified against TGA this session.

NZ.notes: Assumed similar to Australia's framework; not independently checked.

DE.notes: Methylphenidate first-line; dexamfetamine and lisdexamfetamine both approved as second-line/adult options.

sources: ANSM (French National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety) - 2025/2026 Authorizations
FR.notes: Historically Tier 2/3 with restrictive methylphenidate-only policies, France moved to Tier 1 following the 2025/2026 approval of XURTA (lisdexamfetamine) with full marketing authorization, granting access to amphetamine-based treatment.

sources: DARWIN EU / Lancet Regional Health-Europe study
NL.notes: Dexamfetamine and lisdexamfetamine both in active clinical use; adult prescribing is often off-label but real and tracked in national health-record studies.

SE.notes: Sweden has a highly progressive ADHD treatment model. Lisdexamfetamine (Elvanse) is approved for both children and adults. Dexamphetamine (Attentin) is available. Methylphenidate and atomoxetine are standard.

sources: ADHD-Europe AISBL 2021 Survey on Diagnosis and Treatment
European Medicines Agency (EMA) - DARWIN EU ADHD Medication Utilisation
IT.notes: Italy remains highly restricted. Amphetamine-based medications are strictly prohibited. Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Equasym) and atomoxetine are the only approved treatments, and adult prescription is notoriously difficult, with frequent national stock shortages reported.

AT.notes: Elvanse, compounded amphetamine sulfate, and dexamfetamine (Philla) all prescribable via narcotic prescription. Source is a patient advocacy org, not the Austrian regulator directly, though it cites specific legal prescribing mechanisms.

BE.notes: Dexamfetamine approved and used, though dispensing is restricted to hospital pharmacies rather than all retail pharmacies.

DK.notes: Denmark was one of the first adopters in the European Decentralised Procedure for lisdexamfetamine (Elvanse/Aduvanz). Dexamphetamine (Attentin) is also approved for cases where lisdexamfetamine is insufficient.

NO.notes: Norway fully covers ADHD medications. Lisdexamfetamine is marketed as Aduvanz/Elvanse and dexamphetamine (Attentin) is available. Like Sweden and Denmark, it provides comprehensive access to both stimulant classes.

FI.notes: Finland participated in the UK-led decentralized procedure for lisdexamfetamine (Elvanse) and maintains standard Nordic availability. Dexamphetamine (Attentin) is also registered.

CH.notes: Lisdexamfetamine and dexmethylphenidate (Focalin) both available; included in an EU-wide prescription-database study.

sources: Takeda/Shire Pharmaceuticals: Elvanse/Tyvense European Decentralised Procedure Authorisation
IE.notes: Ireland offers broad access. Lisdexamfetamine is marketed under the brand name Tyvense (rather than Elvanse). Methylphenidate and Atomoxetine are standard first and second-line treatments.

sources: Takeda/Shire Pharmaceuticals: Elvanse European Decentralised Procedure Authorisation
AEMPS (Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices) CIMA database
ES.notes: Spain offers full access to standard European ADHD medications. Lisdexamfetamine (Elvanse) was approved via the UK MHRA European Decentralised Procedure. Methylphenidate (Concerta, Rubifen) is widely prescribed as a first-line treatment.

sources: PMC10932761 (Practical clinical guidelines and pharmacological treatment for ADHD in Asia, 2023)
Japanese Guidelines for Diagnosis and Treatment of ADHD, 5th Edition (2022)
JP.notes: Japan approves OROS-methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine (LDX), atomoxetine, and guanfacine extended release for ADHD. LDX is available as third-line treatment. Strict controlled-substance regulations limit prescribing but do not prohibit amphetamine-class medications.

KR.notes: Methylphenidate available; amphetamine-class prohibited. Not independently re-verified against a Korean regulatory source.

sources: PMC8863856 (Utilization of Drugs for ADHD Among Young Patients in China, 2010-2019)
PMC10932761 (Practical clinical guidelines and pharmacological treatment for ADHD in Asia)
CN.notes: Only methylphenidate and atomoxetine are available for ADHD treatment in China. Methylphenidate is the most frequently prescribed medication, with atomoxetine as second-line. Amphetamine-class stimulants are not approved.

HK.notes: Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Ritalin LA, Concerta) is the standard prescribed treatment. Amphetamine is classified as a dangerous drug alongside methamphetamine under Hong Kong law; Adderall specifically is not approved for domestic use.

IN.notes: Methylphenidate available; amphetamine-class prescribing inconsistent across states. Not independently re-verified against Indian regulatory sources this session.

NP.notes: Nepal's official banned-drug list explicitly bans amphetamine and its combinations. The public DDA registry evidence reviewed here supports atomoxetine registration, but not methylphenidate or amphetamine-class stimulant approval.

sources: INFARMED (National Authority of Medicines and Health Products, Portugal)
PT.notes: Lisdexamfetamine (Elvanse) and Methylphenidate (Concerta, Ritalin) are approved but strictly classified as controlled psychotropics. Dexamfetamine is not separately authorized but lisdexamfetamine is actively prescribed.

sources: SÚKL (State Institute for Drug Control, Czech Republic)
EMA Elvanse Patient Information Leaflet Data
CZ.notes: Czechia approves lisdexamfetamine (Elvanse) alongside standard methylphenidate and atomoxetine formulations, bringing them into Tier 1 access for Central Europe.

sources: The exponential increase in the number of prescriptions for ADHD medication between 2012 and 2022 in Poland in patients aged 5–59 years: a pharmacoepidemiological study (ResearchGate)
PL.notes: Methylphenidate (e.g., Medikinet) is the most prescribed ADHD medication. Atomoxetine is also approved and increasingly used. There are no approved amphetamine-class stimulants available for ADHD in Poland.

sources: RELEXXII Methylphenidate HCl Extended-Release Tablets for ADHD
GR.notes: Methylphenidate (e.g., Ritalin, Relexxii, Concerta) is the approved first-line stimulant for ADHD in Greece. Amphetamine-class medications like lisdexamfetamine are not locally approved; patients entering Greece with these prescriptions require special Schengen certificates.

sources: ADHD diagnoses more than triple in 5 years - news | ERR
EE.notes: Methylphenidate (Medikinet) is the primary subsidized ADHD stimulant in Estonia, with recent expansions in adult subsidies. Amphetamine-class medications are not generally approved or prescribable locally.

sources: Global Trends in ADHD Medication Use: Multiple Contexts and Rising Concerns—A Narrative Review (PMC)
IS.notes: Icelandic Medicines Registry data and multinational reviews confirm the utilization and approval of methylphenidate, dexamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine (Elvanse), and atomoxetine.

sources: Ref: A.19 Methylphenidate – attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (Romanian Society of Child and Adolescent Neurology and Psychiatry)
RO.notes: Methylphenidate (specifically Concerta) is authorized and strictly classified as a high-risk drug in Romania, acting as the standard stimulant option in their ADHD treatment protocol. No amphetamines are approved.

CL.notes: Methylphenidate and Lisdexamfetamine are clinically available for ADHD treatment under strict 'receta cheque' (check prescription) requirements. Atomoxetine is approved, though it has previously faced market supply adjustments. Amphetamine-based stimulants like Adderall (mixed salts) or pure dexamphetamine are not typically registered for clinical use in Chile.

sources: Journal of the Pakistan Medical Association
PK.notes: Methylphenidate (e.g., Ritalin) is widely available and used clinically for ADHD. Atomoxetine is also available (e.g., brand name Attenttra). Amphetamine-based stimulants like Lisdexamfetamine or mixed amphetamine salts are not standardly available through official clinical channels in Pakistan.

sources: Directorate General of Drug Administration (DGDA) Bangladesh
BD.notes: Methylphenidate is registered and available under brands like Alaradate and Methyphen. Atomoxetine is also widely available through major local manufacturers such as Square, Incepta, and UniMed UniHealth. Amphetamine-based stimulants like lisdexamfetamine are generally not registered for clinical use.

MY.notes: Doctors can legally prescribe Methylphenidate. Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine) is also approved and available under tight psychiatric control via the Ministry of Health Malaysia.

SG.notes: Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta, Medikinet) is the most widely prescribed first-line option. Health authorities expanded options by officially making Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine) available for prescription.

sources: PMC4982593 (Taiwan National Health Insurance database study)
TW.notes: Immediate-release and OROS methylphenidate are the dominant ADHD treatments per national health insurance data. The study didn't address amphetamine-class status directly - absence of mention is suggestive, not confirmed unavailability.

TH.notes: Methylphenidate is fully approved as a Schedule II psychotropic substance. Both short-acting (Ritalin) and long-acting (Ritalin LA, Concerta) formulations are available. Lisdexamfetamine is classified as a Category 1 narcotic with no recognized medical use - it is illegal to possess, import, or prescribe. Travelers may carry a maximum 30-day supply of methylphenidate with a valid medical certificate in English. No prior Thai FDA permit is required for methylphenidate travelers.

PH.notes: Methylphenidate is the primary approved stimulant for ADHD. Amphetamine-based stimulants are not commonly registered or approved for ADHD treatment in the Philippines.

VN.notes: Methylphenidate is approved for limited use in psychiatric settings. Amphetamines are strictly controlled and not available for ADHD.

ID.notes: Methylphenidate is clinically approved and available with a local prescription, but it is a strictly controlled psychotropic. Amphetamine-based stimulants are generally classified as Category I narcotics and are banned. Personal import of psychotropics by foreigners is subject to extreme regulatory scrutiny and requires specific documentation; local psychiatric assessment is mandatory for ongoing supply.

KH.notes: There is no evidence of a formal national registry or clinical guidelines approving psychostimulants for ADHD. These medications are not standard in the Cambodian pharmaceutical market.

LA.notes: Methylphenidate is permitted for clinical use but is extremely limited in availability, often requiring procurement through specialty channels or private hospitals in Vientiane. Other ADHD medications such as lisdexamfetamine or atomoxetine are not formally registered or widely accessible.

BN.notes: Methylphenidate is available in the public health system. Amphetamines are generally not part of the standard ADHD formulary.

TL.notes: There is no formal ADHD treatment infrastructure or registered pharmacological ADHD management in Timor-Leste.

SA.notes: Methylphenidate (Concerta, Ritalin) and Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) are SFDA-approved for ADHD. Atomoxetine (Strattera) is also approved and available. Access to stimulants requires a local prescription and is strictly regulated; travelers must obtain electronic clearance via the SFDA Controlled Drug System before arrival.

AE.notes: The official material reviewed confirms a strict controlled-medication framework, but the pages checked here were not sufficient to distinguish domestic ADHD prescribing from traveler import rules or permit-only access.

ZA.notes: Methylphenidate widely used; amphetamine-class prescribing more limited. Not independently re-verified this session.

BR.notes: Lisdexamfetamine (Venvanse) and methylphenidate both prescribable under ANVISA controlled-substance rules.

MX.notes: Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine) is a COFEPRIS-registered Grupo II psychotropic under Mexico's health law - the existence of official government counterfeit alerts confirms it's a genuine registered product, not just theoretically approved. Adderall has no legal equivalent in Mexico. Supply caveat: Takeda withdrew Vyvanse from the Mexican market in 2021 and only relaunched it in February 2026, so 'legal' did not mean 'available' for several years - worth keeping availability and real-world supply as separate questions if this matters for your use case.

NG.notes: Methylphenidate available; no evidence found for approved amphetamine-class ADHD stimulants.

ET.notes: Official drug list includes methylphenidate and atomoxetine. Real-world availability appears limited.

CD.notes: No reliable information found regarding ADHD medication approvals.

TZ.notes: Methylphenidate appears available; amphetamine-class approval not confirmed.

KE.notes: Methylphenidate appears available; amphetamine-class approval not confirmed.

MM.notes: Methylphenidate is the primary stimulant used in clinical settings for ADHD, but availability is highly centralized in major urban medical centers and often subject to significant supply chain interruptions. Non-stimulants like atomoxetine and alternatives like lisdexamfetamine are generally unavailable through standard pharmacies.
